newsitem.title: UK: Uk Conservatives brace for election defeat.
newsitem.headline: Uk Conservatives brace for election defeat.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major vowed on Tuesday to fight until the bitter end of Britain's election campaign and brushed aside talk that a crushing defeat could trigger a power struggle within his Conservative party.
Opinion polls show the main opposition Labour party of Tony Blair on course for a landslide win in Thursday's election, ending 18 unbroken years of Conservative rule.

Taking a Conservative defeat for granted, newspapers speculated on how quickly Major would step down and whether the prime minister's flat at 10 Downing Street would have to be extended to make it big enough for Blair's three children.
But a defiant Major insisted all was still to play for and said he was concentrating all his efforts on "ensuring a Conservative victory on Thursday".
"There is a very large number of people who, whether they have made up their mind or not, haven't declared what their mind is," Major told BBC radio.

He said people would judge the government on its five-year record. Measured by inflation, unemployment, growth in living standards, competitiveness or any other standard, Britain was clearly in far better shape than it was in 1979 or 1992.
"I believe people will make up their mind, in a mature democracy, on the record of what has happened and perhaps most relevantly of all, in the plans for the future," he said.
Blair, who has force-marched his party from the left to the centre of British politics since he became leader, repeated his mantra against complacency.

"From now until the close of the polls on Thursday night, we will work night and day to tell the British people of our contract with them, to show them who we are, what we stand for, what they can expect from an incoming Labour government.
"We will fight for each and every vote, in every corner of Britain," he told a news conference.

Blair said he would spend the last hours of the six-week campaign ramming home the message that Labour's policy commitments on health and education would make a difference, even though it has pledged to stick to tight spending limits.

"This is my contract with the British people -- my bond of trust with them. I ask them to judge me and us upon it, hold me to it. The buck will stop with me. What I promise, I will deliver," Blair said.
At the Conservatives' news conference, Major and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine warned afresh that a Labour government would lead to higher taxes and inflation.
"This country is sleepwalking into the sort of disastrous policies that Labour in power has always been responsible for," Heseltine said.
Major quickly denied Heseltine's turn of phrase suggested the ruling party was braced for defeat. "I don't believe Michael believes we will lose the election," Major said.
A Gallup poll in Tuesday's Daily Telegraph newspaper showed Labour with a lead of 22 points over the Conservatives.
Its lead has barely faltered during the campaign, and Gallup's figures would translate into an unprecedented 265-seat majority in the 659-seat parliament.
Newspapers speculated that Major would announce his decision to step down within hours of a defeat but that he would stay on for two or three months to secure an orderly succession.

"I will quit as leader," the pro-Conservative Daily Express trumpeted on its front page. The Financial Times, which on Thursday gave lukewarm backing to Blair, said Major was under pressure to hang on until the autumn because an immediate leadership election could tear the party apart.
Fears that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) might try to disrupt the election grew on Tuesday after a new spate of bomb alerts closed main airports and motorways in southern England.
The IRA has claimed responsibility for a string of small explosions and false alarms during the campaign that have played havoc with Britain's transport network.
